newsitem.title: FRANCE: France deficit may hit 3.4-3.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: France deficit may hit 3.4-3.5 pct.

text.p: Early signs indicate France's public deficit as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) for 1997 will be a little above 3.4 to 3.5 percent, a government source said on Friday.
"What we know already is there was slippage in the early part of the year, which puts us a little bit beyond 3.4-3.5 percent but these are only first indications," the source said.
This would mean France would overshoot the Maastricht treaty target for qualifying for monetary union which limits public deficits to three percent of GDP for 1997.

"We have to be very careful with estimates at this stage of the year," the source said, adding that France would do everything in its power to respect the commitment to launch monetary union on time on January 1, 1999.
The source said the decision to be taken next year by the European Union on which countries can join the single currency would be taken "on the basis of 1997 and the trend of 1998."
The source said, in an apparent reference to Germany, the goal "was not to do worse than our neighbours." "Our aim is to remain more or less in line."
"We will not to get to three percent (in 1997) but it is certain that we are on the path toward reducing public deficits from 1997," the source said.
"What would be totally unreasonable would be to increase public deficits," he said.

New French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who campaigned against imposing further austerity to qualify for monetary union, has said the country's finances are in a serious state and has ordered an independent audit which is to report its findings on July 21.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Thursday France would definitely not reach the three percent target but he stressed the country had no intention of letting public deficits run out of control.
Strauss-Kahn has said the government planned to maintain the level of 1997 public deficits left by its conservative predecessors.
